unit.title: Shapes and Symmetry
unit.blurb: Line and rotational symmetry, parts of a circle, regular and irregular polygons, congruent shapes, and 3D shapes with their nets.
unit.subject: maths

O1.t: Identify lines of symmetry and the order of rotational symmetry of 2D shapes.

O2.t: Know the parts of a circle and classify polygons, including regular polygons.

O3.t: Recognise congruent shapes and identify corresponding sides and angles.

O4.t: Identify and describe 3D shapes, their faces, edges and vertices, and match them to nets.

p: Many road signs and company logos are **symmetrical**. A 'give way' triangle looks the same if you flip it over a vertical line, and a car wheel cover looks the same after you turn it a little.
Look at a regular hexagon (like a honeycomb cell). How many ways can you fold it so the halves match? How many times does it look the same in one full turn? Try it before you read on.
A mirror line makes each point's image the same distance on the other side.

qq.prompt: Which capital letter has a vertical line of symmetry?
qq.hint: Imagine folding it down the middle.

options.fb: Fold down the middle: the halves match.
S has rotational symmetry but no line.

p: A shape has **line symmetry** (reflective symmetry) if a line divides it into two halves that are mirror images. When folded along the line, the halves match exactly. We draw lines of symmetry as dashed lines.
p2: This T-shape has **one** line of symmetry (vertical). A rectangle has 2; a square has 4; a regular hexagon has **6**.

p: A shape has **rotational symmetry** if it looks exactly the same more than once during a full turn (360°) about its centre. The **order** of rotational symmetry is the number of times it looks the same in one full turn.
p2: Every shape looks the same after a full turn, so order 1 means **no** rotational symmetry.
A regular polygon with n sides has n lines of symmetry and rotational symmetry of order n.

qq.prompt: What is the order of rotational symmetry of a regular pentagon?

errs.fb: It looks the same 5 times in a full turn.

qq.hint: How many times does it fit onto itself in a full turn?

lesson.t: How do I find the symmetry of a shape?
p: Step 1: Lines: imagine folding (or use tracing paper); test vertical, horizontal and diagonal lines.
Step 2: Rotation: trace the shape, turn the tracing about the centre and count how many times it fits in one full turn.
Step 3: Record: number of lines, and the order (1 = no rotational symmetry).
Step 4: Check with the rule for regular polygons.

lesson.q: Describe the symmetry of a parallelogram (not a rectangle or rhombus).
steps: Folding along any line never matches the halves
the slanted sides don't line up
A half turn (180°) fits it onto itself

0 lines; order 2
lesson.a: 0 lines of symmetry, rotational symmetry of order 2

lesson.q: Describe the symmetry of a kite.

no other turn fits it onto itself
lesson.a: 1 line of symmetry, order 1 (no rotational symmetry)

lesson.q: Shade the fewest extra squares so that the pattern has 2 lines of symmetry (one vertical, one horizontal).

p: The diagonals of a rectangle and a parallelogram are not lines of symmetry.
Designers use rotational symmetry for wheels, fans and logos so they look balanced when turning.
Line symmetry: the shape folds onto itself along the line.
Rotational symmetry order = number of times it looks the same in a full turn.
Order 1 means no rotational symmetry.

p: A bicycle wheel has a hub in the middle, spokes going out to the rim, and the tyre touches the road at just one point.
Which parts of the wheel match the words centre, radius and circumference? What is special about the road? Think about it before you read on.
The **radius** goes from the centre to the edge; the **diameter** goes right across through the centre, so diameter = 2 × radius.

p2: The road is a **tangent** to the wheel. A spoke is like a **radius**. The diameter is the longest possible chord.

p: A **polygon** is a closed 2D shape made of straight sides. A **regular** polygon has all sides equal **and** all angles equal; otherwise it is **irregular**.
p2: Triangles: **equilateral** (3 equal sides), **isosceles** (2 equal sides), **scalene** (no equal sides), and **right-angled**.
A rhombus has equal sides but not equal angles – so it is not regular. A rectangle has equal angles but not equal sides – not regular either.

Step 4: Use the correct word for each part of a circle.

captions: Look at a bicycle wheel.
There is a hub in the middle.
Thin spokes go from the hub out to the rim.
A spoke goes from the hub to the rim.
Is it most like a radius, a diameter, or a chord?
Pause the video and decide.
A spoke is a radius.
It goes from the centre of the circle to the edge.
The hub is the centre, and the rim is the circumference: the distance all the way round.
Remember: the diameter goes right across the circle, through the centre.
It is 2 times the radius.
If the radius is 8.5 centimetres, the diameter is 2 times 8.5, which is 17 centimetres.
Two more words.
A chord is a straight line that joins 2 points on the circumference.
A tangent is a straight line that touches the circle at exactly 1 point.
A flat road is a tangent to a wheel.
A diameter is a special chord.
It is the chord that goes through the centre.
Your turn.
The longest chord of a circle is called the what?
Pause the video and decide.
The longest chord is the diameter.
A chord gets longer as it moves towards the centre, and it is longest when it passes through the centre.
A polygon is a closed 2D shape with straight sides.
We name a polygon by its number of sides.
3 sides: a triangle.
4 sides: a quadrilateral.
5 sides: a pentagon.
6 sides: a hexagon.
8 sides: an octagon.
10 sides: a decagon.
One is missing from the table.
What is the name of a polygon with 7 sides?
Pause the video and try it.
A polygon with 7 sides is a heptagon.
A regular polygon has all its sides equal, and all its angles equal.
It needs both.
A square is regular: 4 equal sides, and 4 right angles.
A rhombus has 4 equal sides, but its angles are not all equal.
So it is irregular.
A rectangle has 4 equal angles, but its sides are not all equal.
It is irregular too.
Here is the method.
Step 1: count the sides, to name the polygon.
Step 2: check whether all the sides, and all the angles, are equal.
If so, it is regular.
Step 3: for a triangle, compare the sides.
3 equal sides is equilateral, 2 equal sides is isosceles, and no equal sides is scalene.
Step 4: look for a right angle.
A circle has a radius of 7 centimetres.
One chord is 10 centimetres long.
Could another chord be 15 centimetres long?
The longest chord is the diameter.
The diameter is 2 times 7, which is 14 centimetres.
15 is more than 14.
So no: a chord of 15 centimetres is impossible.
A triangle has sides of 6 centimetres, 6 centimetres and 9 centimetres.
Name it.
2 sides are equal, so it is an isosceles triangle.
Another triangle has angles of 90 degrees, 40 degrees and 50 degrees.
It has a right angle, and all 3 angles are different.
So it is a right-angled scalene triangle.
A regular decagon has a perimeter of 45 centimetres.
How long is each side?
A decagon has 10 sides, and in a regular polygon they are all equal.
45 divided by 10 is 4.5.
Each side is 4.5 centimetres.
Is a rhombus with sides of 4 centimetres a regular polygon?
Here is Aya's working.
Which line goes wrong first?
Line 2 is wrong.
Regular means equal sides and equal angles.
The angles of a rhombus are not all equal, so it is not regular.
Equal sides are not enough.
Always check the angles too.
You can find polygons everywhere.
Bees build their honeycomb from hexagons, which fit together with no gaps.
A stop sign is a regular octagon, so drivers can recognise it by its shape alone.
And the British 50 pence coin has 7 sides.
The sides are slightly curved, so that the coin rolls smoothly inside a machine.
One last question.
A regular quadrilateral is a square, a rhombus, or a rectangle?
Pause the video and answer.
It is a square.
Only a square has 4 equal sides and 4 equal angles.
To remember: the parts of a circle are the centre, radius, diameter, circumference, chord and tangent.
The diameter is 2 times the radius, and it is the longest chord.
Polygons are named by their number of sides.
Regular means all sides equal, and all angles equal.

p: Two shapes are **congruent** if they are exactly the same shape **and** size. One fits exactly on top of the other – you may need to turn (rotate) it or flip (reflect) it.
p2: Shapes that are the same shape but a different size are **not** congruent (they are similar).

p: In congruent shapes, matching parts are called **corresponding** sides and angles. Corresponding sides are equal; corresponding angles are equal.
If triangle ABC is congruent to triangle XYZ (written in matching order), then A ↔ X, B ↔ Y, C ↔ Z; side AB = XY, BC = YZ, CA = ZX; angle ABC = angle XYZ.
p2: Here triangle XYZ has been rotated: XY = 4 cm matches AB = 4 cm, so X ↔ A and Y ↔ B.

qq.prompt: Two squares have sides 5 cm and 5 cm, one turned 45°. Are they congruent?

lesson.t: How do I decide if shapes are congruent?
p: Step 1: Check the shapes are the same type with the same number of sides.
Step 2: Match up the corresponding sides (same lengths) and angles (same sizes) – turn or flip in your head.
Step 3: If every pair of corresponding sides and angles is equal, the shapes are congruent.
Step 4: Write corresponding vertices in matching order.

LM = 4 cm
P ↔ K and S ↔ N, so PS = KN = 3.5 cm

third letters match

lesson.a: A and B are congruent; C is not

Which are congruent?
A and B have the same 3 lengths.
The order does not matter, so A and B are congruent.
Every side of C is 2 times as long.
C is the same shape, but bigger.
It is not congruent to the others.
Two equilateral triangles have sides of 3 centimetres and 5 centimetres.
Are they congruent?
Here is Noor's working.
Which line goes wrong first?
Line 2 is wrong.
Congruent needs the same shape and the same size.
These triangles have different side lengths.
So they are not congruent.
Factories depend on congruent shapes.
Every screen protector for one model of phone is congruent, so it fits any phone of that model.
A copy of a key must be congruent to the original.
If it is even slightly different, the lock will not open.
And in a jigsaw, each piece fits only one hole: the hole that is congruent to it.
One last question.
One rectangle is 4 by 6.
Another is 6 by 4.
Are they congruent, or not congruent?
Pause the video and answer.
They are congruent.
The second rectangle is the first one, turned a quarter turn.
To remember: congruent shapes are identical in shape and in size.
They may be turned or flipped.
Corresponding sides are equal, and corresponding angles are equal.

p: A 3D shape can be drawn from different directions: the **front view**, the **side view** and the **top view** (plan). For a square-based pyramid the top view is a square with its diagonals; the front and side views are triangles.

captions: Look at packaging in a shop.
Cereal comes in a cuboid.
Tennis balls come in a cylinder.
And some chocolate bars come in a triangular prism.
How many faces does a triangular prism have?
Pause the video and count them.
There is a triangle at each end.
That is 2 faces.
Between them there are 3 rectangles.
2 plus 3 makes 5 faces.
Remember 3 words.
A face is a surface of the shape.
An edge is a line where 2 faces meet.
A vertex is a corner.
A cube has 6 faces, 12 edges and 8 vertices.
A prism has the same cross-section all the way along.
A triangular prism has a triangle at both ends.
A pyramid has a flat base, and triangle faces that meet at one point, called the apex.
Your turn.
How many vertices does a square-based pyramid have?
Pause the video and count them.
The square base has 4 corners.
Then there is 1 more at the apex.
4 plus 1 makes 5 vertices.
Here are the numbers for some common shapes.
A cuboid has 6 faces, 12 edges and 8 vertices, the same as a cube.
A triangular prism has 5 faces, 9 edges and 6 vertices.
A square-based pyramid has 5 faces, 8 edges and 5 vertices.
A tetrahedron is a pyramid with a triangle base.
It has 4 faces, 6 edges and 4 vertices.
Here is a check for shapes with flat faces.
Faces plus vertices, minus edges, always equals 2.
For the cuboid: 6 plus 8 minus 12 is 2.
We can draw a 3D shape from different directions: the front view, the side view, and the top view, which is also called the plan.
Stand a cylinder upright.
From the front it looks like a rectangle.
From the top it looks like a circle.
Your turn.
A cone stands on its base.
What does its top view look like?
Pause the video and decide.
From above, you see the round base as a circle, and the apex as a dot at the centre.
A net is a flat shape that folds up to make a 3D shape.
This cross is made of 6 squares.
The row of 4 squares wraps round to make 4 sides.
The other 2 squares fold over, to make the top and the bottom.
It is a net of a cube.
Here is the method.
Step 1: decide if it is a prism or a pyramid, and name the shape of its base.
Step 2: count the faces, then the edges, then the vertices.
Work in order: top, bottom, then around the sides.
Step 3: check with faces plus vertices minus edges equals 2.
Step 4: for a view, imagine looking straight at the shape from that direction.
Count the faces, edges and vertices of a pyramid with a hexagon as its base.
Faces: 1 hexagon and 6 triangles.
That is 7 faces.
Edges: 6 around the base, and 6 going up to the apex.
That is 12 edges.
Vertices: 6 on the base, and 1 apex.
That is 7 vertices.
Check: 7 plus 7 minus 12 equals 2.
Correct.
A shape has a triangle as its front view.
Its side view is a rectangle, and its top view is a rectangle.
What is it?
It is a triangle from one direction, and rectangles from the others.
It is a triangular prism, lying on one of its rectangle faces.
How many edges does a square-based pyramid have?
Here is Omar's working.
Which line goes wrong first?
Line 2 is wrong.
There is an edge from every corner of the base up to the apex.
That is 4 edges, not 1.
4 plus 4 is 8.
A square-based pyramid has 8 edges.
The Great Pyramid in Egypt is a square-based pyramid.
It was built about 4,500 years ago, and it is about 139 metres tall.
Drink cans are cylinders.
A cylinder is strong, it is easy to hold, and cans stack neatly on top of each other.
And a classic football is stitched from 32 flat panels: 12 pentagons and 20 hexagons.
One last question.
A shape with flat faces has 7 faces and 10 vertices.
How many edges does it have?
Pause the video and work it out.
Faces plus vertices minus edges equals 2.
7 plus 10 is 17, and 17 minus 2 is 15.
It has 15 edges.
It is a prism with a pentagon at each end.
To remember: a prism has the same cross-section all along.
A pyramid comes to a point, the apex.
Count faces, edges and vertices in order.
For flat-faced shapes, faces plus vertices minus edges equals 2.
The front, side and top views show a shape from 3 directions, and a net folds up to make it.
